claims.statement: On the slope of Mount Mahendra, Hanumān folds his hands to the Sun, to Mahendra, to Vāyu, to Svayambhū and to all beings, and resolves to go south.
Growing vast to leap the ocean, he presses the mountain with his arms and feet; it trembles, and its trees shed every flower until the mountain seems made of flowers.
Hanumān tells the vānaras he will go to Laṅkā like an arrow loosed by Rāma.
Having spoken, he leaps up with great speed, without a second thought.
His shadow on the salt sea, ten yojanas wide and thirty long, follows the son of the Wind like a bank of white cloud.
The Ocean, mindful that the Ikṣvāku king Sagara raised him, resolves that Hanumān must not sink for want of rest, and speaks to the golden-navelled mountain Maināka hidden under the water.
The Ocean reminds Maināka that Indra set him there as a bar over the asuras of Pātāla, standing across the gate of the underworld.
Maināka rises from the water at once, trees and creepers on it, its golden peaks shining like a hundred suns against the sky.
Hanumān, taking the risen mountain for an obstacle in mid-ocean, throws it down with his chest as wind drives a cloud.
Pleased, the mountain takes a human form on its own peak and asks him to rest on its peaks and eat its fruit, for the Ocean, raised by Rāma's line, would repay that kindness.
Maināka honours Hanumān as the son of Vāyu, the Wind, saying that to honour him is to honour his father.
In the Kṛta age the mountains had wings; Indra cut them off with his vajra, but the Wind hurled Maināka into the ocean and so kept its wings whole, which is why Maināka honours the Wind's son.
Hanumān says he is pleased and counts the hospitality as given, but time presses and he has promised not to stop; he touches the mountain with his hand and goes on into the sky as if laughing.
Indra, pleased, grants Maināka freedom from fear for helping Hanumān on his hundred-yojana leap.
The gods, gandharvas, siddhas and great sages ask Surasā, mother of the serpents, to stand in Hanumān's way for a moment in a fearsome form, to learn his strength and resource.
